terminal.screen_rows.note: 80 columns is not directly counted -- in the 1984 Computer Chronicles recording the camera shows what appears to be the whole screen, with the right edge at or just beyond the frame edge, and the machine is an IBM PC, whose text mode is 80x25; this is the source terminal.width already draws its own 80-column figure from. The bottom row of that screen carries the communications program's function-key legend, which persists while DIALOG's output scrolls above it and leaves 24 rows for DIALOG's text; that is where 24 comes from. A 1970s National Agricultural Library memo on DIALOG describes a Hazeltine 2000 CRT at approximately 27 visible rows; that figure is mid-1970s, and the memo's claims are unverified -- the underlying ALIN issue has not been found. It is recorded here as an earlier, unadopted candidate value, not as a source for this entry.

terminal.display_mode.value: printout (default, every line persists and the pane scrolls), screen (only the last terminal.screen_rows lines are kept), or paper (every line persists, restyled as a fixed-pitch sheet)
terminal.display_mode.claim: The reader can choose among three ways output is kept and shown; in the period the terminal decided this.
terminal.display_mode.note: Printout mode corresponds to a printing terminal's paper; screen mode corresponds to an unbuffered CRT. Switching into screen mode discards everything above the last screenful; switching back does not restore it. Paper mode restyles the retained scrollback as a sheet and hides everything outside the stream. Registered separately from terminal.screen_rows, which carries the row count itself.

render.format5.layout.value: Blue Sheet sample record, CRIS-only lines
render.format5.layout.claim: A full record prints as a fixed sequence of labeled fields and blocks, following the one surviving sample record.
render.format5.layout.decision: HNRIMS lines omitted for CRIS-only records (inferred); absent optional fields omit their labels (chosen); one INVEST line per IN (chosen); SP= (Sponsor Code) is also HNRIMS-only per footnote 3 on the field table and is folded out of the PN/AS/DS line along with AT=, ID=, NC=, N1=, and the HNRIMS SUPPLEMENTARY DATA block. Leading spaces were measured on 2026-09-09 directly against the raw SAMPLE RECORD HTML (fixtures/SOURCES.md, fixtures/bluesheet-sample-1998.txt), not against render5()'s own output: the grid header and its four rows indent 8 spaces; the 'GENERAL' line has 49 leading spaces; the 'PRIMARY CLASSIFICATION ... CLASSIFICATION' line has 14; the four SPECIAL CLASSIFICATION rows (XHMR, S2540, S2550, S3110) indent 9 spaces, with the code and label rendered as one field (`${code}   ${label}`) padded to 50 columns so the percent lands at column 59 on every row regardless of code length -- that scheme reproduces the XHMR row exactly, which pad(code,8) + pad(label,42) does not; the PROGRESS line indents 'PROGRESS:' 2 spaces, matching the OBJECTIVES/APPROACH/KEYWORDS label lines. AN= and the two header lines are the only exact leading-space matches by construction (their <td> cells hold a bare literal space with no artifact to strip). Still unreproduced, and left that way because the greedy-fill/single-space render.headings.join algorithm genuinely cannot produce them: the sample's PH=/GH= lines separate the first code/label pair with a stray non-  byte (0xA6) and double the space before every later pair, and PH='s word-wrap breaks at different points than this reconstruction's greedy fill.

value.algorithm: greedy fill, full-justify all but last line

render.text.justify.claim: Paragraph text -- objectives, approach, keywords, publications, progress -- is filled and stretched to a fixed line width.
render.text.justify.note: algorithm chosen; width measured over the OB, AP, DE and PR cells directly from the raw SAMPLE RECORD HTML (fixtures/SOURCES.md), decoding   to a plain space and removing exactly render5()'s own added indent for each row (1 leading space for continuation rows and for /PR's rows, 2 for the label row of a textBlock() call): every full-justified continuation line comes out to 65 characters; the widest line of all is the APPROACH label row at 66. Trial, 2026-09-09: reran render5.ts's own justify(text, width, stretch) algorithm in isolation against the sample's TI text and its OB/AP/PR narrative (reconstructed by collapsing each sample line's words to a single-spaced blob, since the visible multi-space runs in most sample lines are the full-justify stretching itself, then re-wrapping with the algorithm under test). At width 65, called directly for TI (not width - 1), TI's break reproduces the sample's exactly ('...DESIGNED TO' / 'MODIFY LIPID METABOLISM'). Every OB/AP/PR continuation line (28 of 30 checked rows, all of PR's 24 and all but the first row of OB and AP) also reproduces exactly at width 65. The two rows that do not match are the OBJECTIVES: and APPROACH: label rows themselves (63 and 66 measured characters respectively, not 65). Two causes fit that observation and neither is established: the sample may leave label rows unstretched (its OBJECTIVES: row is 63 characters, short of any width), or textBlock() glues the label into the word list it full-justifies so the label's trailing space is stretched like an inter-word gap. Either way the mismatch is unrelated to the width value, is present at any width, and is out of scope here since OB/AP/DE/PB/PR are not exercised by either given test (fixtures/bluesheet-sample-1998.txt marks them '# not-exercised'). Given the near-total reproduction and the TI break holding exactly, width 65 is adopted and TI's call is decoupled from width - 1 to width, called directly.

render.headings.join.claim: When a classification field carries more than one heading, the headings print joined by a semicolon and a space.

terminal.pacing.claim: Printed output arrives at 120 characters per second, a speed documented for DIALOG access in 1984-1988; no source records the speed of a File 60 session.

sources.locator: printed p. 28, section D, Online Communication: 30 or 120 characters per second as the common terminal speeds

ALIN v.14 no.3 (March 1988), printed p. 12, Karl Schneider, "Saving Search Money": "1200 baud or 120 bytes/sec" in a DIALOG print-cost model; "2400 baud access to DIALOG is now or will soon be available". Checked against the page image 2026-09-10.

terminal.pacing.note: Statement of absence: the speed of any 1990-1994 File 60 session was not found by a search of this project's sources, a search of the 89 ALIN OCR files, and one web search, on 2026-09-10. The sources cited here state speeds at which DIALOG was reached in and around the anchor period; none of them is a record of a File 60 session, and the anchor-period sources it consulted are printouts, which record no timing. 120 characters per second is chosen from that documented range, not measured from any session. src/terminal/sink.ts reads cps from this value and emits printed characters at that rate. The ALIN v.15 no.1 (1989) dial-in figure (1200 or 2400 baud) was checked against the page image on 2026-09-10 and is the access speed of ALF, NAL's bulletin board, not of DIALOG; it is not cited here. The prompt stays live during output: src/terminal/sink.ts never disables the input while a line paces out at this rate, and a line entered before the output finishes is taken up once it does.

terminal.line_editing.value: native single-line editing: character insert, backspace, left and right, paste; no history
terminal.line_editing.claim: Typing uses the browser's own text editing: insert, backspace, arrows, paste. Enter submits the line. This is not a simulation of a period terminal's editing.
terminal.line_editing.note: What a 1990 searcher could edit before return is not recorded in any source held; the textarea covers insert, backspace, arrows and paste. The textarea's native editing is the input model, not a simulation of a documented DIALOG editing rule. Enter submission is the app's, not the textarea's own behaviour, and the visible caret is drawn by the app (index.html's caret-color:transparent and the .cursor span); the editing itself is the browser's.

terminal.wrap.claim: A long set line wraps in the browser rather than running off the edge; no source documents how DIALOG itself wrapped long lines.
terminal.wrap.note: wrapping of long set lines is not documented

terminal.scrollback.value: the browser's own scrollbar; no custom scroll chrome
terminal.scrollback.claim: The session stays on screen and can be scrolled back; a 1990s terminal did not keep it.
terminal.scrollback.note: DIALOG sent a character stream. On a printing terminal, output was printed and could not be scrolled back; on a screen it scrolled off the top unless the searcher's own communications program buffered it, which no source in the corpus records.

index.format.value: one JSON file per phrase-indexed field, offsets.json for record spans
index.format.claim: Search terms are looked up in files built for this reconstruction; how DIALOG itself indexed File 60 internally is not known.
index.format.note: DIALOG's own internal index structures are unknown to us; this is a search accelerator built for this reconstruction, not a claim about how DIALOG indexed File 60

inspect.mode.value: click-to-inspect panel: What was printed, How DIALOG names it, The bytes in the NARA file, Where the file came from, Why it prints this way
inspect.mode.claim: Clicking a printed line opens a panel explaining how that line was produced, back to its position in the archival file.
inspect.mode.note: Inspect mode is modern scholarly apparatus with no DIALOG-period precedent. The panel's cards are named for a reader: the record's Format B bytes and its archival container are one card, "The bytes in the NARA file"; the rest are "What was printed", "How DIALOG names it", "Where the file came from" (tape provenance) and "Why it prints this way" (transformation evidence). The panel can be hidden behind a toggle at the aside's edge; hiding it changes nothing in the session -- it is a display choice over the same character stream.

terminal.keyboard_inspect.value: stamped spans are tabbable; Enter/Space opens inspect; Escape returns focus to the prompt; Alt+I inspects the most recent typed record line
terminal.keyboard_inspect.claim: The inspect panel can also be reached from the keyboard: Tab to a line and press Enter, or press Alt+I for the line typed most recently.
terminal.keyboard_inspect.note: Keyboard-only operation for a mouse-only affordance (click-to-inspect) that DIALOG itself never had, so there is no DIALOG-period rule this could be inferred from.

terminal.restart.value: a button (and Alt+R) discards the session's sets and open file, empties the printout and inspect panel, and returns to an empty prompt
terminal.restart.claim: A button restarts the session; in the period a searcher logged off and dialed in again.
terminal.restart.note: DIALOG had no clear command; ending a session and starting another meant LOGOFF, then dialing in again. Restart is implemented as app wiring (src/app/main.ts constructs a fresh DialogSession and calls DomSink.reset()), not a DIALOG-layer concept, and it prints nothing into the character stream -- no LOGOFF accounting block (not implemented) and no new BEGIN banner, since neither corresponds to any DIALOG output this control actually causes.

nara.tape.fy1994_media.value: two 1/2-inch open reel, 9-track, 6250 bpi, EBCDIC, non-labeled; NARA copy 3480 cartridge, EBCDIC, blocked 5040, OS standard labels
nara.tape.fy1994_media.claim: The physical tape chain for this file is inferred from NARA's record of a neighboring year's tape, not documented for this file itself.
nara.tape.fy1994_media.note: FY 1994 has no per-file validation statement of its own; these are the FY 1991 statement's media facts (already cited by nara.conversion.control_bytes), applied to FY 1994 by inference -- see src/app/corpora.ts's FY1994 tape comment

nara.tape.fy1994_accession.claim: The transfer record under which NARA received this file is not known; nothing on screen states one.
nara.tape.fy1994_accession.note: NAID 1204533 (fixtures/ACCEPTANCE.md) identifies the digitized text NARA now serves, not the transfer accession under which the physical FY 1994 tape was received. The FY 1991 validation statement's own accession is NN3-164-93-001 (CRIS Format B specification, February 1990, source note) -- the nearest documented instance, and it is not established whether FY 1994's accession is the same one. Statement of absence: not found by this project's method in the sources it consulted; would be resolved by the NARA Catalog's RG 164 series/accession record for the FY 1994 transfer, not yet located.

nara.file.fy1988_fixity.claim: The FY 1988 archival file this profile was measured against is this many bytes and hashes to this sha256.
nara.file.fy1988_fixity.note: Matches the pattern of nara.file.fy1994_fixity. FY 1988's own file is not loaded by this app and is not present on every machine that runs it (unlike FY 1994's, which src/loader/cli.ts refuses to index without); packages/cris-formatb/fixtures/fy88-9000001.bin is a real slice of AN 9000001 cut from the file, not a full-file substitute. Verified against the file on this machine on 2026-09-10 (sha256, byte count, first and last line all match).

nara.tape.fy1988_accession.claim: The transfer record under which NARA received the FY 1988 tape is named in its validation statement.
nara.tape.fy1988_accession.note: Unlike nara.tape.fy1994_accession (not found), FY 1988's own validation statement gives this directly -- which is why the file carries the RG310 designation rather than RG164's.

nara.file.fy1988_header_record.claim: The FY 1988 file opens with a single header line recorded outside any project record, the same convention as FY 1994's.
nara.file.fy1988_header_record.note: the file's first line, preceding any '$$' record, matching nara.file.header_record's FY 1994 convention. Verified against the file on this machine on 2026-09-10 (sha256, byte count, first and last line all match).

nara.file.fy1988_trailer_record.claim: The FY 1988 file closes with a single trailer line giving the total line and record counts, recorded outside any project record.
nara.file.fy1988_trailer_record.note: the trailer's own two counts, 3153115 (data lines between header and trailer) and 32016 (records), correspond to the FY 1988 column of the CRIS Format B element table (32,016 records, 52,340 IN values). A full-corpus scan on 2026-09-10 (scanRecords over the whole file) found 32,016 records, matching the trailer's own record count; the data-line count was not independently re-tallied. Like nara.file.trailer_record's FY 1994 value, the two counts run together with no separating space -- this reconstruction's earlier reading of the FY 1994 trailer as space-separated was a misreading corrected by a direct byte read, not a real difference between the two files' trailers. Verified against the file on this machine on 2026-09-10 (sha256, byte count, first and last line all match).

formatb.encoding.fy1988_sc_percent.value: under fy1988, an SC value's text is split at every 0xA0 0x02 separator: the first segment is the code, the second the label, a third the percent
formatb.encoding.fy1988_sc_percent.claim: In the FY 1988 file, an SC value's percentage is carried inside the SC block itself instead of in a separate SN line.
formatb.encoding.fy1988_sc_percent.note: documented from a full-corpus measurement, not inferred from one record: parsing every SC value in all 32,016 records under the fy1988 profile on 2026-09-10 found 59,385 SC values, every one splitting into exactly three segments (code, label, percent) at two 0xA0 0x02 separators, with zero exceptions. AN 9000001's own SC field ('SC XFRS  <A0><02>Forestry Related' / '  <A0><02>100%' / ' <AC>S0613 <A0><02>Other Western Conifers' / '  <A0><02>100%') is one instance of this, not the sole evidence. A source formerly cited here as the CRIS Format B specification, February 1990, section 6.1, was actually a section of this project's own unpublished design document, not the 1990 specification, and has been dropped.

nara.file.header_record.claim: The file opens with a single header line recorded outside any project record.
nara.file.header_record.note: the file's first line, preceding any '$$' record; scanRecords opens no record on it and reports its text separately

nara.file.trailer_record.claim: The file closes with a single trailer line giving the total line and record counts, recorded outside any project record.
nara.file.trailer_record.note: the trailer's own two counts, 3384620 (data lines between header and trailer) and 34090 (records), match scanRecords' full-corpus scan; scanRecords closes the record open before this line and excludes the line itself from that span. The value is a direct byte read of the corpus at line 3384622, which shows the two 9-digit counts concatenated with no separating space rather than a space between them.

capability.notice.value: one modern line beneath the prompt, shown only after EXPAND, PAGE, DISPLAY SETS, LOGOFF, SORT, PRINT, KWIC, or TYPE by accession number
capability.notice.claim: A note below the prompt says when a real DIALOG command is not reconstructed; DIALOG printed no such note.
capability.notice.note: A command DIALOG documented for File 60 but not implemented here is recognized by the parser (returns { cmd: "unsupported" }, src/dialog/parser.ts) instead of being treated the same as a typo. The session (src/dialog/session.ts) prints nothing for it into the character stream; the app (src/app/main.ts) shows the one-line notice outside the stream, so it never reaches scrollback, a copied selection, or the copy trailer.

index.word.tokens.value: split on spaces and on punctuation other than the hyphen; digits are tokens; keys are uppercased
index.word.tokens.claim: A search term is split at spaces and punctuation other than the hyphen; digits count as terms; everything is matched in capitals.
index.word.tokens.decision: the 2001 book states what a word-indexed search term may contain (any single word, number, or alphanumeric expression) and that punctuation inside one must be replaced with a proximity operator to search it; this reconstruction reads that as punctuation not being part of the indexed token and drops it at split time, rather than indexing the punctuation character itself, which is the alternative it does not adopt.

index.word.stopwords.claim: Nine common words (an, by, for, from, of, the, to, with, and) are never indexed as search terms.

sources.locator: page 206, the nine Dialog stop words (lines 21687-21709)

index.word.stopwords.note: the 2001 book documents this list for DIALOG generally, not for File 60 in 1994 specifically; that it held for the 1994 export is inferred, not itself documented for that year.

index.word.hyphen.value: indexed whole and as its parts
index.word.hyphen.claim: A hyphenated word is indexed as one term and as each of its parts, so a search can match either.
index.word.hyphen.decision: indexed whole (e.g. GENE-TRANSFER) and as its parts (GENE, TRANSFER); the alternative, whole only, is not adopted. No source held states which DIALOG itself did.

index.word.shards.value: one file per first character: A-Z, 0-9, and _ for anything else
index.word.shards.claim: The word lists are split into files by first letter so a search loads only the part it needs; DIALOG's own index shape is not known.

map.TX.composite.claim: The TX search field merges three fields' text on this corpus; the Blue Sheet documents a fourth this corpus never carries.
map.TX.composite.note: the Blue Sheet's footnote 6 documents /TX as the union of /AP, /NR, /OB and /PR. /NR is the HNRIMS narrative tag NA; its FY 1994 count in this corpus is 0 (measured, index-builder.ts's word-index build), so on this corpus /TX is built as AP + OB + PR. The missing /NR component is a consequence of the corpus, not a choice made here.

index.sh.phrase_only.value: SH= built as a phrase index only
index.sh.phrase_only.claim: Subject headings are searched as whole phrases only; one source calls two of their fields word-searchable, a reading not adopted here.

sources.locator: elements 46 and 47 (PH, GH): 'Word and Phrase', SH= 'searches literal only'

index.sh.phrase_only.conflicts: Format B's own element table calls PH and GH 'Word and Phrase' under SH=, while its entry for SH= itself says the field 'searches literal only', i.e. phrase-indexed. The phrase-only reading is what this build implements; the disagreement is recorded here rather than resolved silently.

terminal.width_rule.claim: A thin vertical line marks the 80-column edge of the printout; the terminals drew no such line. It is hidden when the window is narrower than the printout.
terminal.width_rule.note: The documented terminals were width-limited (terminal.width, 80 columns) and a modern browser window is wider, so the printout's right edge is marked with the same neutral rule colour the panels use. index.html .printout{border-right} and the @container query on .terminal-pane enact it; no colour or CRT claim is made. Chosen: a modern convenience with no historical counterpart.

proto.select.precedence.claim: Without brackets, NOT is worked out first, then AND, then OR; brackets change the order, innermost first.

sources.locator: SELECT, "Logical and Proximity Operators" / "Order of Processing"

proto.select.precedence.decision: no anchor-period source states the order of processing, so this reconstruction follows the 2001 book's stated order (parentheses, then proximity, then NOT, then AND, then OR) instead of refusing mixed operators.
proto.select.precedence.note: proximity operators are out of the slice, so only the NOT, AND, OR part of the order is exercised

proto.select.boolean.claim: Searches can be combined with AND, OR and NOT; NOT takes a set on each side and cannot start a statement.

sources.locator: p. 185, "? COMBINE (8 AND 12) NOT 15" answered "16 35 (8 AND 12) NOT 15"

proto.select.boolean.decision: NOT is binary (spec 7.12); a leading NOT does not parse. In 1978 these combinations were made with COMBINE and a set-number legend, not SELECT's own AND/OR/NOT words; COMBINE is out of this slice, and the SELECT form of 1984 onward is what this reconstruction implements.

proto.select.truncation.claim: A question mark at the end of a search word finds every word that starts with it, counted together on one line.

sources.locator: Basic Index, SELECT examples: 'S DIET?/PR', 'S CHOLESTEROL?/TX'
Sample Search/Output, p. 184: '? SELECT LOBSTER?' printing '3 14 LOBSTER?'

proto.select.truncation.note: Only the single trailing '?' is implemented. Statement of absence: no other truncation form (bounded '??', spaced '? ?', internal '?') was found for File 60 by grepping 'truncat', '??' and '? ?' across the 2001 manual text and the stripped 1998 Blue Sheet text on 2026-09-10; the parser refuses those forms rather than reading them as a single '?'. A PREFIX=value? truncation (Blue Sheet: 'S PO=OHIO STATE UNIV?') is documented and not implemented here.

proto.error.unmatched_parens.claim: An unclosed bracket has a documented reply in a later manual; this reconstruction still prints its own short form.

sources.locator: SELECT, the note after "To use more than one level of parentheses"

proto.error.unmatched_parens.decision: recorded, not printed. The OCR renders the leading characters ambiguously (»>) and the page image has not been checked; spec 7.10's simulated form (a question mark plus the offending token) is still what the session prints. Printing this text is an open decision.
proto.error.unmatched_parens.note: this is the only error text found in any source held; spec 7.10's statement that none had been read is superseded for this one case

proto.expand.display.claim: EXPAND prints a ref number, an items count, and an index term in three fixed columns.
proto.expand.display.decision: the column positions are inferred from DATABASE magazine's own re-typeset figure 4, not read directly from a DIALOG-issued transcript; the twelve-row window and the E-numbering are documented in the 2001 chapter (see proto.expand.window and proto.expand.enumbers), and are only stated here as a note.
proto.expand.display.note: the unprefixed EXPAND browse (no PREFIX=) is served here from the merged, re-sorted union of the /TX, /TI, /DE and /PB word-term lists, an inference: the Blue Sheet's own Basic Index is /AP /DE /NR /OB /PB /PR /TI /TX, and /AP, /OB and /PR already sit inside /TX on this corpus.

proto.expand.window.claim: EXPAND shows twelve index terms at a time, with the term you entered usually third on the list.

sources.locator: figure 4, the entered term at E3

proto.expand.window.decision: spec section 13 listed the window shape as unknown; the 2001 chapter settles it (a twelve-line page, the entered term usually third), and 1988 figure 4 brackets the placement at E3 rather than merely later. The entered term is listed whether or not it has any items.

proto.expand.collation.value: byte order of the uppercased keys
proto.expand.collation.claim: The EXPAND list sorts terms in plain character order; no source records DIALOG's own index collation.
proto.expand.collation.note: Statement of absence: DIALOG's collation for File 60 was not found by reading the EXPAND sections of the 1998 Blue Sheet, the 1988 DATABASE figures, the 1994 Curso pages, and the 2001 book, on 2026-09-10.

proto.sort.command.claim: SORT takes a set number, an item range or ALL, and one or more field codes, each optionally reversed with a comma and D.

sources.locator: Sorting: sortable field list and the example 'SORT S13/ALL/PN'

proto.sort.newset.claim: SORT builds a new set, described as 'Sort' followed by the command's own argument in capitals.

sources.locator: SORT: 'The SORT command creates a new, sorted set...' and the example printing 'S2 60 Sort Sl/ALL/AU'

proto.sort.newset.note: The source's own two worked examples print 'Sort' with only its initial capitalised, followed by the rest of the argument in capitals ('S2 60 Sort Sl/ALL/AU'; 'S2 147 Sort S1/ALL/SA,D/ST') -- reproduced here exactly rather than normalised to 'SORT' or 'sort', since the source shows the same mixed-case form twice, not once as a plausible typo.

proto.sort.fields.claim: The Blue Sheet lists nineteen sortable fields; sorting on one this corpus has no value for leaves every record's key empty, not an error.

sources.locator: Sorting: sortable field list, heading 'SORTABLE FIELDS / EXAMPLES'

proto.sort.fields.note: Five of the nineteen listed codes (AG, AI, CG, ID, SP) are HNRIMS/ICAR codes this CRIS-only FY 1994 export carries no value for -- no built phrase index exists under any of them (PHRASE_PREFIX_TAGS, src/loader/corpus-format.ts). A sixth, AT, is also unbuilt under its own two-letter code: this corpus's only index for that Format B tag lives under the composite search code A1 (map.AT), not under the bare tag AT the Blue Sheet's Sorting section lists, so sorting on AT also returns every record's key empty. All six are accepted, not refused -- refusal (the simulated '? <FIELD>' form) is reserved for a code outside this nineteen-field list entirely, e.g. 'SORT S1/ALL/OB'.

value.moreLine: Enter P or PAGE for more

proto.expand.page.claim: PAGE shows the next twelve terms; PAGE- returns to the page before it and un-stars the originally entered term.

sources.locator: EXPAND, "Entering a PAGE command will display the next 12 entries" and "the original EXPAND entry is no longer asterisked"

proto.expand.page.note: the "Enter P or PAGE for more" line prints only when a further page of terms exists.

proto.expand.enumbers.claim: Each EXPAND row gets a ref number E1 through E50, restarting at E1 after E50.
proto.expand.enumbers.note: A ref number stays usable in SELECT until the next EXPAND with a term.

sources.locator: EXPAND, "A sequence of E numbers runs from E1 to E50 ... the next 12 sequential entries will appear, with the numbering reset to E1"

proto.expand.enumbers.decision: a new EXPAND naming a term erases the previous list and its ref numbers (2001: "erases the previous list"); PAGE and PAGE- keep the same list and continue the same E-number sequence.

proto.selectsteps.sets.claim: SELECT STEPS numbers a separate set for each term as well as for the whole search.

sources.locator: figure 2: "?ss expert(w)system? ?/de and scheduling" answered S1 6605 EXPERT/DE
PDF page 99 (printed page 113): "?ss technolog?(W)transfer?/ti" answered S1 4322 TECHNOLOG?/TI, S2 1330 TRANSFER?/TI, S3 252 TECHNOLOG?(W)TRANSFER?/TI

proto.selectsteps.sets.note: the alin-1992 citation is only a name for SS as a period search command, not a transcript of its output; the set shape itself comes from the 1988 and 1994 sources.

proto.selectsteps.processing.claim: SELECT STEPS prints the word Processing before its set lines.

sources.locator: figure 2, the line "Processing" printed before S1

proto.selectsteps.processing.note: whether a plain SELECT also printed Processing first is not recorded in any source held; this reconstruction's SELECT does not print it.

proto.displaysets.table.claim: DISPLAY SETS reprints the table of sets made since the session's last BEGIN.

sources.locator: figure 3, the set table under OneSearch

the DISPLAY SETS section: "?display sets" prints the header and every set, "?ds s1-s2" prints a range, and the list shows "the set number, the number of items retrieved, and the contents of each set" for the sets created since the last BEGIN

proto.displaysets.table.note: the same set-line layout as SELECT's, reusing the two header lines; the File column belongs to SET DETAIL ON, which is out of the slice, and both DS 1-3 and DS S1-S3 are accepted because both forms are documented.

proto.logoff.template.claim: LOGOFF prints a date/time/user line, then one costed line per charge, ending with the estimated total.
proto.logoff.template.note: BEGIN opens with the same date/time/user line.
proto.logoff.template.decision: the Descriptors and Prints lines the 1978 session shows belong to commands (EXPAND-adjacent descriptor display, PRINT) outside this slice and are not reconstructed; only the connect-time line, one line per TYPE format actually used, and the two total lines print.

sources.locator: '? logoff' block: '          28feb78 14:17:38 User316', '  $2.60  0.065 Hrs File60  12 Descriptors', '  $3.50  35 Prints', '  $6.10  Estimated Total Cost', 'LOGOFF 14:17:45'

rates.file60_1998.claim: Connect time costs $0.25 a minute; TYPE format prices are mostly $0.60, with formats 1, 6 and 8 free.

sources.locator: Rates section: 'Cost per minute: $0.25'; Types/Prints table, $0.60 for every format except 1, 6 and 8 at $0.00

rates.file60_1998.note: no 1990-1994 rate card is held -- statement of absence, not found in dataset-cards/research/cris-dialog/sources/ by the acquisition and review of 2026-09-09. Formats 1, 5 and 6 are implemented, so LOGOFF now prices real TYPE lines for all three (1 and 6 both free); typeByFormat's remaining entries (2,3,4,7,8,9,10,12,13,14) never price anything this reconstruction actually prints, and are carried because the 1998 sheet documents them for the file as a whole. A user-defined display-code format is never priced from this table: the Rates section of bl0060_19980423153346.html has no row for a display-code list -- a statement of absence, not found there on 2026-09-10 -- so accounting.ts's typeByFormat lookup falls through to its own zero default for that format string.

proto.accounting.combination.claim: This reconstruction prices a session using the 1978/1988 LOGOFF template with the 1998 rate card.
proto.accounting.combination.note: No single source gives both the template and rates for the same year, so this key is labeled inferred rather than documented. Pricing never bills anything, and BEGIN's opts.accounting flag (spec 7.9) can switch it off entirely.

proto.session.user_number.claim: The user number in the session's first line is chosen; no source records one for this reconstruction's searcher.

proto.session.clock.claim: The printed date and time are the reader's own and make no historical claim.
proto.session.clock.note: src/app/main.ts passes the system clock; the evidence-test harness and the recorded cast (scripts/cast.ts) pass a fixed clock instead, so their output stays reproducible.

render.format1.layout.claim: Format 1 prints only the record's DIALOG accession number.

sources.locator: PREDEFINED FORMAT OPTIONS table, row '1 DIALOG Accession Number'

render.format6.labels.claim: Format 6 prints six labelled fields, in this order: agency, project number, period, investigator, performing organization, and location.

sources.locator: Sample Search/Output, p. 185: the `16/6/1` and `16/6/2` blocks

render.format6.labels.note: The 1978 EPA session predates this reconstruction's 1990-1994 anchor period; it is pre-anchor evidence for the six labels and their order, not for the corpus record itself.

render.format6.columns.claim: Where each label sits on the line is this reconstruction's choice; the one surviving example is typeset, so its columns are not evidence.

render.userformat.codes.claim: A comma-separated list of display codes can be typed after TYPE to build a custom output, the same way TYPE S3/IN,OB/1-5 does.

sources.locator: USER-DEFINED FORMAT OPTIONS: 'Display codes listed in the Search Options tables can be used to customize output, e.g., TYPE S3/IN,OB/1-5'
worked example `?type s2/ti,au/1-5` prints the item header `2/TI,AU/l` (the OCR's 'l' is '1')
